title: Esther 1:13–22
context: The angry king consults wise men who know the times, law, and judgment, named as seven princes of Persia and Media who see his face. The king asks what should be done to Vashti according to law. Memucan answers that her deed will be known to all women and will spread contempt for husbands, and he proposes an unalterable royal commandment: Vashti may never again come before the king, and her royal estate should go to another better than she, so that wives throughout the kingdom will give their husbands honor. The advice pleases the king and the princes, and letters go out to every province, in each people’s writing and language, “that every man should rule his own house”. The unit is court politics and an imperial decree, not a treatise on marriage written for a later debate. The notes report Memucan’s argument and the edict soberly, without culture-war framing and without deciding that the narrator either endorses or satirizes every word. The book still does not name God. That Vashti’s removal opens a place for another queen is the clear narrative result; hidden-providence readings of that opening are common in both traditions and remain shared and hedged, not a new contrast. Both traditions read the close of the chapter as the legal and political setup for chapter 2.

verses.text: Then the king said to the wise men, who knew the times (for it was the king’s custom to consult those who knew law and judgment;
verses.arminianNotes:
The king turns to the wise men “who knew the times”, and the verse explains that it was his custom to consult those who knew law and judgment. The crisis is at once handed to counselors. What “the times” means here is left as the text gives it: men thought qualified in law and in the moment, not a cue to import a later theory of court astrology unless the verse had said so.

Arminian readers take the consultation as a real royal habit, the king seeking advice after his anger, not acting on the refusal alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see a court that proceeds by custom and by counsel. The wise men are those who know law and judgment, and the next verses will name them.

Both traditions keep the line as narrative procedure, without a contrast over the phrase “the times”.

verses.text: and next to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king’s face, and sat first in the kingdom),
verses.arminianNotes:
Next to him are “Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king’s face, and sat first in the kingdom”. They are the inner circle, named as those who have access and first rank. Memucan, last in the list, will speak. No further biographies are invented for the seven.

Arminian readers take the seven princes as real high officials of Persia and Media, the men whose counsel the king will follow.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the names as a court roster, men who see the king’s face and sit first, the body that will hear the question and approve the decree.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the list and do not turn the seven into a symbol.

verses.text: “What shall we do to Queen Vashti according to law, because she has not done the bidding of the King Ahasuerus by the eunuchs?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king asks, “What shall we do to Queen Vashti according to law, because she has not done the bidding of the King Ahasuerus by the eunuchs?” The question is put in legal terms: what does the law require after a refused command. The refusal is already treated as a public failure to do the king’s bidding.

Arminian readers hear a real legal question put to the counselors, the king binding the next step to law rather than to a private outburst alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note that the case is framed “according to law,” the same court that earlier had a law about drinking now asked to judge the queen.

Both traditions keep the question as the narrative puts it, without deciding more about Persian law than the book itself will claim.

verses.text: Memucan answered before the king and the princes, “Vashti the queen has not done wrong to just the king, but also to all the princes, and to all the people who are in all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus.
verses.arminianNotes:
Memucan answers that Vashti “has not done wrong to just the king, but also to all the princes, and to all the people who are in all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus.” Memucan widens the offense from a private insult to a threat against the whole realm. That widening is Memucan’s argument, not yet a narrator’s verdict, and the notes leave it as counsel spoken before the king.

Arminian readers take the speech as a courtier’s real plea, enlarging the case, and they do not have to accept his enlargement as the only just reading of her refusal.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also distinguish the counselor’s words from the book’s own voice. Memucan claims a wrong done to princes and people in all the provinces; the story will show how far that claim is used.

Both traditions report the argument without a party fight over Vashti, and without culture-war framing of the widening charge.

verses.text: For this deed of the queen will become known to all women, causing them to show contempt for their husbands when it is reported, ‘King Ahasuerus commanded Vashti the queen to be brought in before him, but she didn’t come.’
verses.arminianNotes:
He warns that the queen’s deed will become known to all women, causing them to show contempt for their husbands when it is reported that King Ahasuerus commanded Vashti the queen to be brought in before him, but she didn’t come. The feared result is contempt in ordinary households, a spread of the queen’s example. The report he imagines is accurate as to the fact of the refusal.

Arminian readers hear Memucan’s fear as a political argument, not as a revealed law about marriage, and they keep the verse in the mouth of the counselor.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the contempt warning as Memucan’s forecast, a piece of court rhetoric that will justify a wide decree.

Both traditions refuse to lift the speech out of the story and make it a standalone rule, and they invent no contrast over it.

verses.text: Today, the princesses of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen’s deed will tell all the king’s princes. This will cause much contempt and wrath.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Today, the princesses of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen’s deed will tell all the king’s princes. This will cause much contempt and wrath.” The danger is pressed still closer: the princesses will speak, and contempt and wrath will follow among the princes themselves. Again the speaker is Memucan.

Arminian readers take the warning as a continuation of the same plea, aimed at moving the king, not as an independent lesson in household order.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the princesses and the threatened wrath inside the counselor’s speech, the rhetoric by which a royal marriage dispute is made a matter of state.

Both traditions handle the line soberly and do not turn it into a modern debate about men and women.

verses.text: “If it pleases the king, let a royal commandment go from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, so that it cannot be altered, that Vashti may never again come before King Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate to another who is better than she.
verses.arminianNotes:
Memucan proposes that a royal commandment be written “among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, so that it cannot be altered,” that Vashti may never again come before the king, and that her royal estate be given “to another who is better than she.” The irrevocable law of the Persians and the Medes is the book’s own way of describing such decrees, and it will matter again later; a larger question of historical Persian jurisprudence is not settled beyond what this narrative assumes. The phrase “better than she” is Memucan’s wording for a successor.

Arminian readers take the proposal as a real legal device in the story, a permanent ban and a transfer of estate, opening a vacancy without further violence being named here.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear an unalterable written law as the means chosen to settle the queen’s fate, and they leave “better than she” as the counselor’s comparison, not as a moral score the narrator has already issued.

Both traditions note, as shared and hedged ground, that this proposal will clear the way for another queen, without turning the counsel into a secret message.

verses.text: When the king’s decree which he shall make is published throughout all his kingdom (for it is great), all the wives will give their husbands honor, both great and small.”
verses.arminianNotes:
When the decree is published throughout the great kingdom, Memucan says, “all the wives will give their husbands honor, both great and small.” The hoped-for result is honor in every household, the other side of the contempt he has feared. The sentence is still his advice, offered to please and to persuade.

Arminian readers keep the promised honor in the mouth of the counselor, a political hope attached to a royal edict, not a verse detached as a free-standing household code.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the published decree and its hoped-for effect as Memucan’s close. Honor to husbands is what he says the edict will produce; the book does not pause to confirm that it did.

Both traditions report the aim soberly, without culture-war use of the line, and without a party contrast over it.

verses.text: This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did according to the word of Memucan:
verses.arminianNotes:
This advice pleased the king and the princes, and the king did according to the word of Memucan. The counsel is accepted by the king and by the princes together, and it is carried out. The court speaks with one voice here; the next verse will send the letters.

Arminian readers take the agreement as a real political decision, the king choosing Memucan’s plan, a human choice with wide public effects.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the court consenting as one, the word of Memucan becoming the king’s act, the means by which Vashti’s place is emptied.

Both traditions keep the verse as the hinge between advice and decree, still without a contrast over hidden providence, which remains a reading of the larger story, not a code in this line.

verses.text: for he sent letters into all the king’s provinces, into every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language, that every man should rule his own house, speaking in the language of his own people.
verses.arminianNotes:
Letters go out “into all the king’s provinces, into every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language, that every man should rule his own house, speaking in the language of his own people.” The edict is translated across the empire and tied to a man’s rule in his house and to his own language. The notes report that content as the decree’s wording, soberly, and do not use it as a text for a later social argument.

Arminian readers take the letters as a real imperial mailing, the refusal in Susa now made a law for every province, an overreach some readers have seen in the very breadth of the order, though the narrator does not pause to say so.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear an empire-wide command in every language, the household rule and the native tongue named together, and they leave any judgment on the wisdom of the policy as a matter of reading the story, not as a doctrine to be forced here.

Both traditions close the chapter on that published word, the way now open for chapter 2, with hidden-providence readings of the vacancy still shared and hedged.
